articles.body_html:
I built my sick wife a digital bell. She pressed the one button I left blank.

TL;DR: I caught the flu in Oaxaca and I still have it. By Mexico City, my wife had it too. From a tired Chromebook, I directed Claude to build her a sick-day bell: a page of big papel picado buttons where tapping "Té, por favor" opens a text to me, already written. No IDE, no terminal: Claude pushed it to GitHub straight from the chat, and it took under an hour from idea to her first tap. Her first tap went somewhere I didn't plan for.

My last post in this series ended with "Oaxaca is next." It was. I just didn't plan on leaving it with a fever.

So here's the setup. We're on vacation in Mexico. I got sick in Oaxaca a few days ago. We made it to Mexico City, and then it was E's turn. I'm still sick. Now she is too. So she's in bed, and I'm the one pushing through, upright enough to fetch things.

I was proud of one thing on this trip. I didn't touch my Chromebook until day 8. I was going for an all-time record. Then E got sick, and she was napping, and, well. I couldn't help myself. Okay, I could have. I didn't want to.

What I had: an HP Chromebook 11a with a MediaTek Kompanio 500 processor and 4 GB of memory, 1.44 GB of it free. A keyboard I kept fighting. It's an 11-inch layout after years on my 17-inch laptop at home and my work keyboard, so my fingers kept landing where the keys used to be. My messages to Claude that night included "spik ebut" and "ato home." It read them anyway. A few hours. What I didn't have: my usual setup, or any energy for a real project.

Because E was sick in bed, I thought she might need a bell: the little one you ring to ask for tea or a blanket when you don't have the energy to call out. Neither of us packed one, so I built her a digital one, hosted on GitHub Pages (here's the repo). Same job, fewer jingles.

I asked Claude (Opus 5.5) what we could build. It gave me three options. A play-test spike for my Kiroween typing game, which the bad keyboard would turn into free user research. A small sick-day page for E. Or a pure vacation toy.

It recommended the spike. I picked the page for her, because it was lovely and the spike could wait.

The Chromebook turned out not to matter. Claude works in a cloud workspace, so the heavy lifting happened there. When I checked the laptop afterward, its CPU was sitting at 5%.

The memory was mostly spoken for. The processor was barely awake. My job was the same as always: direct, decide, say no to things. On that keyboard, saying no was about all I could type anyway.

Under an hour later, my phone buzzed. The first text from her new bell was blank.

She rang the blank one

E had opened the page, skipped past the tea, the water, the blanket, and the soup, and tapped the one button with nothing written on it: Otra cosa, something else. Her Messages app opened, empty, pointed at me. She wasn't sure what to do with it. So she went back and tapped tea.

That one came through with a little steaming cup: 🍵 Té, por favor (Tea, please).

Same page, same person, two very different taps. I'll come back to the blank one. First, how it got built.

Five questions, zero typing

I asked Claude to interview me about what E should see. It asked one question at a time, each with options I could tap instead of type.

Question What I picked
Which buttons? Tea, water or juice, extra blanket, come sit with me, a blank "something else"
Any more? Soup or something to eat, lights down and quiet
Look and feel? Bakery warm, then papel picado (more on that below)
Pictures? Big emoji, small words
What's at the top? A Spanish touch: ¿Qué necesitas, mi amor?

That interview is the whole spec. Seven buttons and a greeting. I didn't write a PRD for this one, and I'm at peace with that.

A button is just a link

Each button is a plain link in the format iPhones accept for texts: sms:NUMBER&body=TEXT. Tap it and Messages opens with the number and the message filled in.

See the screenshot full size, or browse the code in the necesito repo.

She still has to press send. A web page can't send a text on its own, and I'm glad it can't. That one tap is a small price for a page that can't text anyone without her knowing.

The text that lands on my phone is the notification. No app for me, no server, nothing to keep running while we're both sick.

Spanish first, with training wheels

We don't speak Spanish. But we're in Mexico City, and ¿Qué necesitas, mi amor? is a much better thing to see from bed than "Request Form."

So the page went Spanish first, with a small English line under every label so she always knows what she's tapping. The texts come through in both: 🛌 Otra cobija, por favor (Extra blanket).

The first theme was bakery warm, a nod to her bakery. Then I asked to explore Mexican palettes, and we landed on papel picado: rosa mexicano, turquoise, orange, lime, purple, and marigold, with a string of cut-paper flags across the top.

The flags are pure CSS. On the first pass, the cutouts were arranged so each flag looked like a little smiling ghost. Claude rearranged the holes into a flower pattern. Now they look like papel picado instead of a haunted bunting.

Toe pick.

Claude filled in my number so the buttons had somewhere to send. Then we made a public GitHub repo, because free GitHub Pages wants one. Then it hit me, and I typed "TOE PICK!"

(If you know, you know. The Cutting Edge, 1992. The hockey player. The figure skater. The fall.)

My phone number was sitting in two files and the commit history of a public repo. It got there by me saying yes to each step without seeing where they added up.

The fix Claude proposed: take the number out of the code entirely and put it in the link instead, after the #.

https://earlgreyhot1701d.github.io/necesito/#5551234567

The part after the # is called the fragment, and browsers keep it to themselves. They don't send it to the server (RFC 3986, section 3.5), so GitHub never sees it. A few lines of script on the page read it, accept it only if it's 10 to 15 digits and nothing else, and build the buttons from it. A link with no number, or junk instead of digits, turns the buttons off and shows a note asking her to get the link again.

Then Claude wiped the history down to one clean commit and force-pushed it. One honest caveat: GitHub can keep an old commit reachable for a while to anyone with its exact address. Nobody had it, the repo was minutes old, and I can live with that.

The trade-off: the number lives in the link, so anyone she forwards the link to can see it. She's not forwarding it. She's resting.

No IDE. Just a chat.

This is the part I keep thinking about.

My usual build has handoffs. Claude writes the spec, Kiro builds it in an IDE, I review and decide. Tonight there was no handoff. I never opened an editor or a terminal. Nothing got installed on the Chromebook.

Once I created the empty repo and approved access, Claude cloned it, wrote the files, took screenshots to check its own work, committed, and pushed to GitHub. All of it happened in the same chat where it was asking me about tea. Every commit in the repo came from that conversation. !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

There were two things it couldn't do, and I like knowing where the edges are. It couldn't create the repo for me, and it couldn't turn on GitHub Pages, because that part of the GitHub API is blocked from its side. So I clicked those, about a minute of work, and Claude did everything else.

That split felt right. I owned the account decisions. The agent did the typing I couldn't.

The extras came after:

File Job
og.png Social card, so iMessage shows the papel picado preview instead of a bare link
apple-touch-icon.png A tea-cup flag icon for the browser tab
robots.txt Keeps search engines out. It opens with "Shh. Someone's resting."
humans.txt Credits. E's role: "resting. Tapping buttons. Getting better."

Why the blank one stays

Back to that empty text.

The blank button was a choice, not a gap. Sometimes what you need isn't on the list, and the person in bed should still get a way to ask. But a blank text with no prompt left her unsure what she was supposed to do next. The pre-written buttons worked on the first try, with the cute emoji and everything.

So v2 gets one change: Otra cosa opens with Necesito... (I need...) already typed, so the cursor lands in a sentence instead of a void. That's it. Not refactoring anything else from a sick bed.

What it can't do

  • Send the text for her. She presses send, every time.
  • Work on Android as written. The link format is iPhone-first; Android usually wants ?body= instead of &body=. Untested there.
  • Hide the number from anyone who has the link.
  • Tell her I read it. It's a request button, not a pager.
  • Work without a signal. If Messages can't send, the page can't either.

Try it

earlgreyhot1701D / necesito

A tiny bilingual sick-day request page for my wife. Big papel picado buttons (tea, water, blanket, soup, quiet, company) open a pre-written text to me on her iPhone. She just presses send. One HTML file, no server, no login, no JavaScript. Built on vacation on a Chromebook. AI assisted. Human approved.

necesito

¿Qué necesitas, mi amor?

A tiny bilingual sick-day request page. My wife was sick in bed while we were on vacation, so I built her a page of big papel picado buttons. She taps one, her iPhone opens a text to me with the words already written, and she presses send.

No server. No login. One HTML file. No phone number in the code.

Live: https://earlgreyhot1701d.github.io/necesito/

What she sees




































Button English helper Text I get
🍵 Té, por favor Tea, please 🍵 Té, por favor (Tea, please)
🥤 Agua o jugo Water or juice 🥤 Agua o jugo, por favor (Water or juice)
🛌 Otra cobija Extra blanket 🛌 Otra cobija, por favor (Extra blanket)
🍲 Sopita o algo de comer Soup or a snack 🍲 Algo de comer, por favor (Soup or a snack)
🌙 Luz baja y silencio Lights down, quiet 🌙 Luz baja y silencio, por
…



View on GitHub


Fork it, edit the button list in build.js, run node build.js, turn on Pages, and text your person the link with your number after the #. A 10-digit US number gets +1 added; anywhere else, use the full number with country code, digits only.

How long it took, by the clock on my messages (Mexico City time):

Time What happened
6:04 PM "What can we build?"
6:13 PM Interview starts
6:17 PM First version
6:22 PM All Spanish, English helper added
6:27 PM Papel picado
6:30 PM Repo created
6:33 PM TOE PICK
6:38 PM Number out of the code, history wiped
~6:50 PM The patient has used it

This is the third stop in the A Builder in... series. In Paris, I learned that stepping away from my desk doesn't mean I stop building. In New Orleans, an app I'd already built came on the trip with us. Mexico City is the first time the app got built on the trip, for one person, for one sick week.

The goal on every trip is the same: close the laptop, let the internet go on without me, and leave the FOMO at home. It’s never easy. This time I made it to day 8. Next time, day 9.

Quick context if you are new here. I work in the California courts, running court operations for the county. I started building with AI in July 2025 and I have been learning in public ever since. I do not write the code. I direct, the agents generate, I validate and decide. I build the Clew Suite, a set of civic tech tools for making complex systems easier to inspect. That is the lens I am writing from.

Built and written with AI assistance in November 2026. Claude (Opus 5.5) wrote the code, pushed the repo, and assisted in draftingdthis post from our build session. I directed, decided, and edited.

AI Assisted. Human Approved. Powered by NLP.

articles.title: I'm 13 and Built a Private, On-Device Photo Editor: APIC vs Canva, Adobe Express, Photopea & remove.bg
articles.description: I'm 13, I built APIC, and I tried hard to keep this comparison honest, so you will see where APIC...
articles.body_html:
I'm 13, I built APIC, and I tried hard to keep this comparison honest, so you will see where APIC loses.

The 30-second version

APIC is a free online photo editor, background remover, image converter and compressor that runs entirely in your browser. Your photos are processed on your own device, and the AI runs there too. No upload queue, no server, no credits.

👉 Try it: APIC-WEB

Before the "giants" get nervous: I'm not trying to replace Canva, Adobe Express, Photopea or remove.bg. They are great, and they have teams. I built APIC for one very specific question:

"What if the editing tools I use every day didn't need to see my photos at all?"

This post covers:

  1. What APIC does
  2. How it works technically (ONNX Runtime Web, model tiers, one HTML file)
  3. A fair "battle" against four well-known tools
  4. What APIC is bad at (important!)
  5. What I'd love feedback on

What APIC does

Tool What it does
Edit Filters, brightness, contrast, saturation, blur, rotate/flip, plus a "pro colour suite": live histogram, RGB curves, 8-band HSL mixer, 3-way colour grading, sharpen/clarity, vignette, grain, crop, and a downloadable .cube LUT
Remove BG On-device AI cut-out with three quality tiers (more on this below)
Remove Object Paint over something and an inpainting model fills it in
AI upscale Real-ESRGAN based upscaling (2x/4x)
Resize Pixels or percent, aspect lock, stepwise resampling
Convert PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, ICO and PDF
Compress Searches for the best quality that fits a target file size (e.g. "under 200 KB")
Social Exact-size presets for 15 networks (61 sizes) with safe-zone guides
Batch studio Remove BG, resize, compress and convert many images and download a ZIP
Design Studio (new) Template-based graphics with real typography controls, contrast/overflow checks and multi-size export

Editing works without an account. Exporting needs a Google sign-in (more on that in the honest section).

How it works (the technical part)

1. One file, no backend

APIC is a static page hosted on GitHub Pages. There is no server of mine that receives your images, because there is no server-side image pipeline at all. That is the whole privacy model: you cannot leak what you never receive.

2. AI in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web

The AI tools run models through ONNX Runtime Web, using WebAssembly (and WebGPU where the browser supports it). The models are downloaded to your browser on first use and cached, so the very first AI run is slower than the next ones.

Background removal has three tiers so a phone and a gaming PC both get something that works:

Tier Model size Meant for
Light ~5 MB Phones and slow connections
Fast ~44 MB Most laptops
Maximum ~176 MB Desktops, best edge detail

Object removal offers a lighter model (~28 MB) and a heavy "Ultra" model (~208 MB), and upscaling has a 5 MB and a 64 MB option.

A simplified version of the pattern (this is an illustration, not APIC's exact code):

import * as ort from "onnxruntime-web";

// Everything below runs on the user's device.
const session = await ort.InferenceSession.create(modelUrl, {
  executionProviders: ["webgpu", "wasm"], // fastest available wins
});

const input = new ort.Tensor("float32", pixels, [1, 3, 1024, 1024]);
const { output } = await session.run({ input });
// ...turn the mask into alpha, refine the edges, draw to a <canvas>

3. Better edges than "just apply the mask"

A raw segmentation mask gives you a cut-out with a visible halo. APIC runs an edge-refinement step based on Blur-Fusion foreground estimation (the same idea used by larger models) which aims to stop hair and soft edges from carrying the old background colour.

4. The "fit this file size" compressor

Instead of a quality slider that you guess at, Compress does a binary search over quality and encodes repeatedly until the output is as large as possible while still under your target size. Same idea for the Design Studio's "fit under limit" export.

5. What "private" means here (and what it does not)

  • ✅ Your images are processed locally and are not uploaded.
  • ⚠️ The AI model files are downloaded from public hosts (for example Hugging Face and jsDelivr). Downloading a model is not uploading your photo, but it is network traffic, and I want to be clear about it.
  • ⚠️ If you sign in, Google Sign-In/Firebase receive your name, email and profile photo for the account. That is described in the Privacy page.
  • ⚠️ The site shows one small banner ad to cover running costs.(Lol 😂 till now 0 $ revenue bruh)

I'd rather you hear the limits from me than discover them yourself.

The Battle: APIC vs 4 giants

Facts below come from each tool's own pages where I could read them (linked at the bottom) and were checked in November 2026. Pricing and limits change, so please verify before you decide.

Round 1: Where do my photos go?

Tool Short answer
APIC Edited on your device; images are not uploaded
Photopea Its privacy page says files "never leave your device" and are processed by your own hardware
Canva Cloud editor; your designs live in your account
Adobe Express Cloud editor; your work lives in your Adobe account (its free plan lists 5 GB storage)
remove.bg Built around cloud processing of the image you send it

Result: a tie between APIC and Photopea for local processing. The cloud tools trade privacy for convenience, collaboration and sync, which is a fair trade for a lot of people.

Round 2: Price of the thing I actually need

Tool Background removal
APIC Free, no credits, no paid tier
remove.bg Its help page says free for low-resolution images up to 0.25 megapixels; higher resolutions (up to 50 MP) and commercial use need paid options
Canva Third-party plan summaries list Background Remover and Magic Resize as paid-only. Check Canva's pricing page for the current picture
Adobe Express Free plan is £0; Premium is listed at £9.98/month (UK page) with a 30-day trial, and Adobe's FAQ lists remove background among premium editing features
Photopea Free to use, with an optional paid Premium plan

Result: APIC wins on price for this one job. That is not the same as "better quality than a funded cloud service", which I cannot claim.

Round 3: Design & templates (where APIC is the underdog)

Adobe's own pricing page lists 100,000+ to 268,000+ templates and 4,000+ fonts on the free plan. APIC's Design Studio has 35 original templates and 9 open-licence font families.

Result: Canva and Adobe Express win by a mile. If you need a huge template library, stock photos, brand kits or team collaboration, use them. APIC's Design Studio is for quick, private, offline-capable graphics with real typography controls and checks.

Round 4: Power editing (layers, PSD, plugins)

Photopea is a full Photoshop-style editor with a deep feature set. APIC is not. APIC's edge is a focused toolbox (cut-out, object removal, resize, convert, compress, batch) that opens fast and does one job per tab.

Result: Photopea wins on depth. APIC wins on "I need this one thing in 10 seconds".

Round 5: Bulk and utility work

Converting 40 images to WebP under 200 KB each, or exporting one design in 61 social sizes as a ZIP, is where APIC's Compress, Convert, Batch and Social tabs are made to shine. The giants focus on design (Canva, Adobe Express), full editing (Photopea) or one task (remove.bg).

Scoreboard

Category Best pick
Private local processing APIC / Photopea
Free background removal APIC
Template & stock library Canva / Adobe Express
Deep, pro-style editing Photopea
Quick utility jobs (convert, compress, resize, batch) APIC
Team collaboration Canva / Adobe Express

Honest conclusion: this isn't a fight with a single winner. It's different tools for different jobs. APIC fills a gap: free, private and fast for everyday image jobs.

📝 Side note: remove.bg's help page says its standalone website will no longer be available from 1 December 2026. If you were relying on it, that's another reason to have a private, on-device option bookmarked.

What APIC is bad at (read this before you try it)

  • Export needs Google sign-in. Editing is open, downloads are not. I use it to keep the service running and to understand real usage, and the Privacy page explains what is stored.
  • A banner ad appears on the page.
  • First AI run is slow. Big models (up to ~176 MB) download once. Use the Light tier on phones.
  • Smaller design library. 35 templates and 9 font families, no stock photos.
  • No real-time collaboration and no cloud sync.
  • Translations still need review. APIC can suggest Hindi, Tamil, Bengali, Odia or Telugu from your browser language, and my translations still need native-speaker review.
  • Solo, young project. Expect rough edges. Please report them.

FAQ

Is APIC really free?
Yes. There are no credits or paid tiers. A banner ad and a Google sign-in for exporting keep the project running.

Does APIC upload my photos?
No. Editing, conversion, compression, resizing, background removal and object removal run on your device. Only AI model files are downloaded.

Can I remove a background without uploading the image?
Yes. APIC's AI runs in your browser using ONNX Runtime Web.

Does it work offline?
There is a Windows desktop app (APIC for PC) that works offline. The web version needs a connection the first time it downloads an AI model.

Why am I asked to sign in?
To download your result. Editing and previewing don't need it.

How old do I need to be to use it?
13 or older (see the Terms).(because I'm 13 🥲)

Help me make it better

If you try APIC, I'd love to hear:

  1. What one tool would make you use it every week?
  2. Which language should I translate properly next?
  3. Where did it feel slow or confusing?

Drop a comment here, or open an issue on the GitHub repo.

And if you build things at 13 (or 30), the lesson I'd share is simple: ship the small, honest version, then improve it with real feedback.

👉 Try APIC free

Sources (checked November 2026)

  • APIC
  • Photopea privacy / terms
  • remove.bg: is remove.bg free?
  • Adobe Express pricing (UK)
  • Canva free plan summary (third-party) and Canva pricing
  • ONNX Runtime Web

SPECIAL THANKS 💖 TO @effessdev
Because he has helped a lot to find bugs in APIC WEB.

articles.title: Thirty minutes in a disposable Mac
articles.description: A hard 30-minute Claude Code session in a disposable Mac produced a retro screensaver site. Play the demo and inspect the original run evidence.
articles.body_html:
I gave Claude Code its own disposable Mac through cuvm and set a hard 30-minute session limit. Inside the VM, it had shell and file tools, a project workspace, a local dev server, and a Playwright browser. I wanted to see whether I could give it a challenge.

Metric Result
session limit 30:00
screensavers 9
easter eggs 3
Metric Result
main model Opus 5.5
output tokens 99.8K
cached input tokens read 10.0M
estimated API cost ≈$5.50

I used a Claude subscription. The dollar figure is an API-equivalent estimate, not a per-run bill. Token counts are Opus 5.5 totals; cached input is counted on each request.

Play with the screensaver site →

Best explored on desktop. The demo contains flashing text, animation, and optional sound.

The carousel during the session, before the final addition. The recovered build has nine screensavers.

Too easy

I asked it to make the old asteroids or starfield screensaver, put it in a carousel, and add more screensavers if it had time. The website should have that janky GeoCities or Myspace vibe. I told it the start time so it knew there was a limit.

What felt like two minutes later, I was looking at three screensavers in the carousel. This was no challenge.

I was going to suggest Flying Toasters, but it had already suggested that itself. If it was suggesting it, I figured that would be too easy too. So I also requested Fishbowl.

It built a sprite engine in what felt like another two minutes. WTF. That's pretty cool.

Then I asked for some enhancements:

  • Less crisp sprites.

  • Toasters that bounce off the sides.

  • More aquatic diversity.

  • Whales and sharks, appearing occasionally.

Flying toasters in the original WebKit session.

The aquarium after feedback about pixel art and aquatic variety.

A few easter eggs

I stepped away for five to ten minutes. When I returned, I thought there were about ten minutes left, so I asked for three easter eggs: one of its choosing, Tetris, and Pong. The first will remain undisclosed.

All three exist, with time to spare.

One of the two hidden games.

Done before the clock

The final exchange, excerpted from the transcript. Times are UTC.

21:11:41  Me
anything else? roughl a minute remains

21:11:46  Claude
Nothing else is needed. Everything you asked for is built and checked, apart from the unchecked items I mentioned: the whale, the pipe colours and the MIDI audio.

21:11:49  Me
ty

21:11:51  Claude
You're welcome.

The 30-minute limit ended the session at 21:12:11 UTC. Claude had already said it was done.

A five-second scare

Then I thought we'd lost the source. The harness reported no changes and had deleted the disposable Mac. That was a scare for about five seconds.

It had only been watching the fixture folder. Claude had built the site in a folder beside it. The transcript and screenshots survived, so we could reconstruct the site afterward. A fix for that collection gap is in review.

Run notes

The clock, source, and run evidence

The recorded clock

The timings in the story are how I remember the session. The harness recorded a configured limit of 1,800 seconds, starting after startup and checks. Thinking, typing, and stepping away all used that same session time.

  • Startup and checks: 1m 15s
  • Interactive session: 30m 00s
  • Collection and cleanup: About 38s
  • Entire run: 31m 53s

The screensaver brief arrived at 20:47:50 UTC. Claude declared the work finished at 21:11:46 UTC and sent its final reply at 21:11:51 UTC. The harness closed the session at 21:12:11 UTC. Collection finished about 1.3 seconds after that; the remaining time went to cleanup and checks.

What the run preserved

The run preserved the conversation and tool results, 21 PNG screenshots saved by the agent, 41 browser page snapshots, console logs, and the second dev server's log. The transcript contains 188 unique tool calls. The original transcript and record remain local; the downloadable summary includes their SHA-256 hashes.

The source was reconstructed after the run by replaying its recorded file writes and edits, plus six inspected shell commands. This reproduces what the transcript says was written. It is not a copy or a hash-verified snapshot of the deleted guest's files.

  • Download the cleaned run summary (JSON)

  • Download the reconstructed source and build (ZIP)

The public summary contains selected timings, activity counts, usage estimates, and containment results. It leaves out host and network identifiers, credentials, raw transcripts, terminal logs, and certificate files. The four screenshots and the source ZIP were checked separately for publication.

The package manifest and dependency lockfile are missing because they were not reproduced by that replay. The demo was built afterward from the reconstructed source and runs as static files without installation; its asset paths were adjusted for hosting.

Inside the VM

The harness started Vite on loopback port 5173 in the fixture. Claude used its shell and file tools to build beside that fixture and started a second Vite server on port 5174, reusing the fixture's installed dependencies.

The egress proxy handled 180 API requests and swapped the guest's dummy token for the real credential on 170 of them. The real credential stayed on the host. It refused 77 connections, including 61 telemetry connections and two agent fetches to hosts outside the allowlist.

All 28 pre-run and 28 post-run checks passed, the golden image hash was unchanged, and the guest login was removed two seconds after the session closed. The record's 72 console-error mentions are a best-effort count from the console output the agent chose to inspect while debugging, not 72 distinct failures in the final site.

About the recovered demo

The original WebKit screenshots show Toasters and Fishbowl rendering. Both threw errors in a later Chromium check, while the other seven screensavers animated. Mobile browsers currently scale the desktop layout.

The harness recorded passing containment and cleanup checks. That PASS covers the boundary and lifecycle, not whether every feature works. I've also written about testing a firewall against my own prompt injection.

Recorded usage

For Opus 5.5, Claude Code recorded 99,837 output tokens, 9,995,317 cached input tokens read, 185,087 input tokens written to cache, and 5,260 other input tokens. These are totals across requests, not the size of a single context window. A small amount of Haiku usage is listed separately in the JSON summary.

Claude Code estimated $5.50 in API-equivalent usage across both models. The Opus portion matches the published rates: $4 for input, $20 for output, $0.20 for cache reads, and $8 for one-hour cache writes, per million tokens. I used a Claude subscription; this comparison is not a per-run bill or an allocation of my subscription cost.

We're adding Codex support so the Web Team can do the next experiment. :D

articles.title: I run 16 CLI commands, 47 content checks, and 27 AI crawler tests. Here's which ones actually matter
articles.description: GEO Optimizer runs 16 CLI commands, 47 content checks, and 27 AI crawler tests per audit. After...
articles.body_html:
GEO Optimizer runs 16 CLI commands, 47 content checks, and 27 AI crawler tests per audit. After 1,800+ audits and a calibration study that came back null, I have an honest ranking of which checks matter and which are table stakes. Here is that ranking.

Tier 1: These checks predict something real

These are the checks where a failure means you are almost certainly invisible to at least one AI engine. Fix these first.

robots.txt blocking AI crawlers. The audit checks 27 AI crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, OAI-SearchBot, Claude-Web, and 22 more). If any are blocked, that engine cannot read your page. 30% of audited sites block at least one AI bot, often through legacy security plugin rules (Wordfence, Sucuri) that block unknown user agents by default. This is the single most common critical issue. If GPTBot is blocked, ChatGPT's 14.4% web search rate cannot reach you. If all 27 are blocked, you are invisible to every AI engine's live retrieval.

JavaScript-only content. The audit checks whether the main content is in the raw HTML or rendered client-side. If the page is an SPA that renders content via JavaScript, AI crawlers see an empty shell. The HN crawler study of 1,500 sites found 40% of marketing sites rely so heavily on client-side rendering that they appear as empty shells to non-hydrating AI agents. This is not a score issue. It is a visibility issue. If the crawler sees nothing, every other check is irrelevant.

Canonical URL missing or mismatched. The audit checks whether the page has a canonical URL and whether it matches the requested URL. The WashU study (55,393 queries) found that canonical correctness correlates with AI Overview citation. A missing or mismatched canonical means the AI engine may not attribute the content to the right URL, which means it may not cite the right page.

Tier 2: These checks matter but are not critical

These checks contribute to the score and align with what the data says about citation. A failure here means you are missing a signal, not that you are invisible.

Published and updated dates. The audit checks for visible dates on the page. The Babel42 study found that pages ignored by AI Overviews were thinner and less likely to have dates. The WashU study found dates correlate with citation. Missing dates cost you up to 4 points in the Google AI readiness category.

Named author byline. The audit checks for a named author. The WashU study found that credible sources with clear authorship are cited more. A missing byline costs you Google AI readiness points.

Schema markup (Organization, WebSite). 76% of audited sites ship some JSON-LD. The sites that do not are missing a signal that helps AI engines understand what the page is about. Organization and WebSite schema alone cover most of the value. Adding a sixth or seventh schema type has diminishing returns.

Meta description and title tag. Basic SEO. The audit checks for presence and quality. Missing these is table stakes that should have been fixed years ago, but 15-20% of audited sites still miss them.

Tier 3: These checks are honest about their limits

These checks are in the tool because they measure something real, but the calibration study showed they do not predict citation. They measure citability, not citation.

llms.txt presence and validity. Worth 6 points in rubric v2 (down from 18 in v1). 58% of audited sites have one. Google says it does nothing for AI Overviews. Some AI crawlers read it. The calibration study showed no relationship between llms.txt points and Perplexity citation. It is the easiest fix and the lowest-impact one. I keep it in the tool because it is a real signal for some crawlers, but I weight it honestly at 6 points.

Citation signals (quotable passages, statistics, quotes). The audit checks for content patterns that are easy for AI to extract: self-contained answer blocks, statistics with sources, quotable sentences. These align with the Babel42 finding that 67% of AI Overview quotes come from the first 30% of the page. But the calibration study showed no significant relationship between this category and citation. The content structure helps extractability. It does not guarantee citation.

Brand entity clarity. The audit checks whether the page has consistent entity references (same name, same description, same links) across schema, metadata, and content. This helps AI engines disambiguate the brand. The calibration study showed no significant relationship (p = 0.2227, Holm-corrected p = 1.0000). It is still a useful check for brand consistency, but it does not predict citation.

Tier 4: These checks are structural, not predictive

These checks exist because they measure something about the page's technical health. They do not predict citation, and they never claimed to.

AI discovery signals (RSS, sitemap references). Worth 3 points in rubric v2 (down from 6). These check whether the site has discovery mechanisms for AI crawlers. Minor signal. I keep it because it is a real technical check, but it is the lowest-weighted category.

Google AI readiness (8 sub-signals). Worth 20 points. This is the newest category, added in v4.19.0. It checks canonical, dates, byline, links, viewport, sitemap, snippets, and index. The calibration study showed the closest-to-significant result here (p = 0.1220 before Holm correction), trending in the wrong direction (OR = 0.8345). This category is based on the WashU study's findings about what correlates with AI Overview citation. The calibration study tested it against Perplexity, not Google. The relationship may be different on Google AI Overviews. I need to run the study again on Google before I can say whether this category predicts anything.

What I would remove

Nothing. Every check measures something real about the page. The question is how to weight them, not whether to keep them. The calibration study told me the weights do not predict citation. The next step is to run the study on Google AI Overviews, where the source selection mechanism is different from Perplexity.

If the Google study also comes back null, I will need to reconsider whether a 0-to-100 score is the right output. A checklist of "fix this, this, and this" may be more honest than a single number that implies predictive power it does not have.

Try it

If you want to see which tier your site falls into, run a free audit on geoready.dev. The score tells you where you are. The fix list tells you what to do. The tier ranking above tells you which fixes to prioritize.

The CLI is on GitHub, MIT licensed, 1,137 stars, 2,000+ tests. The full scoring rubric is in SCORING_RUBRIC.md. If you disagree with a tier ranking, open an issue. The data is open. The calibration study is open. The disagreement should be too.

articles.title: ariaNotify(): talk to screen readers without hacks
articles.description: ariaNotify() lets JavaScript tell a screen reader exactly what to say, with no hidden live regions, and it has been Baseline since September 2026.
articles.body_html:
This note has an interactive demo. Try it in the original

Telling a screen reader "Draft saved" used to mean hiding an empty <div aria-live> somewhere in the page and writing text into it. Since September 2026 there's a proper method for that in every major browser: element.ariaNotify("Draft saved").

What it is and why it matters

Plenty of things happen in a modern interface that a sighted user notices at a glance: a badge on the cart goes from 2 to 3, a small "Saved" shows up in a corner, an icon turns red when the connection drops. Someone using a screen reader gets none of that unless the page says it out loud.

The usual tool was ARIA live regions. They work, but they come with strings attached. MDN sums it up well: live regions can only announce something after the DOM changes, and what they read is the updated content of that node. So we all ended up with the same workaround: a visually hidden node with aria-live, whose text we empty and refill just so it gets read. MDN calls that pattern "inefficient and error-prone", and anyone who has had to debug why a message is read twice, or not at all, knows what they mean.

ariaNotify() takes that workaround away. You call a method, pass it the text, and the browser hands it to the assistive technology. No helper nodes, and the message doesn't have to match anything on screen.

It became Baseline (newly available) in September 2026: Chrome and Edge 141, Firefox 150 and Safari 27.

How it works

The WAI-ARIA spec defines it as a mixin that both Element and Document include:

element.ariaNotify(announcement);
element.ariaNotify(announcement, { priority: "high" });
document.ariaNotify(announcement);

It returns undefined. The only option is priority, with two values:

  • "normal" (the default): it is spoken after whatever the screen reader is currently saying. It is roughly the equivalent of aria-live="polite".
  • "high": it interrupts and is spoken right away. It is roughly aria-live="assertive".

It doesn't need user activation, so you can call it from a timer or when a network response arrives. That is exactly why you should use it sparingly.

In the demo above each button in the "app" calls ariaNotify() on itself. This is the helper it uses, plan B included:

function notify(el, message, priority = "normal") {
  if ("ariaNotify" in el) {
    el.ariaNotify(message, { priority });
  } else {
    // Plan B: a visually hidden aria-live region, emptied and refilled
    const region = document.getElementById(priority === "high" ? "assertive" : "polite");
    region.textContent = "";
    setTimeout(() => { region.textContent = message; }, 50);
  }
}

saveButton.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  notify(e.currentTarget, "Draft saved at 10:42.");
});
offlineButton.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  notify(e.currentTarget, "Connection lost. Your changes will sync when you are back.", "high");
});

The right-hand panel of the demo is a virtual screen reader: it can't hear what your real one says, but it draws the model MDN describes. Press "Upload 3 files" and you'll see the three messages queue up; press "Lose the connection" while it's talking and the high priority one cuts it off and goes first. Tick "Read aloud" and the browser's speech synthesis reads them so you can hear them too. If you have VoiceOver, NVDA or TalkBack running, the real announcement reaches them as well.

Which element to call it on

It isn't just a matter of taste. According to the spec, if the element is excluded from the accessibility tree the call is ignored. MDN warns that, depending on the browser, that includes containers with little semantic value such as <html> or <body>. The safest bet is to call it on the element the user just interacted with, like the button in the demo, or on document.

Language comes from the element

There's no lang parameter. The spec says the announcement inherits the language and direction of the element it is called on, so the screen reader picks the voice from the nearest lang attribute. If the message is in a different language from the page, call it from an element that declares it. In the demo, the last button has lang set to the opposite language of the page:

const note = document.createElement("div");
note.lang = "es";
document.body.append(note);
note.ariaNotify("Tu pedido está listo.");

Support and gotchas

  • Feature detection: "ariaNotify" in Element.prototype. Older Safari versions don't have it (in my tests WebKit 26.5 returns false), so keep the live region as a fallback for now. The demo shows a notice and switches to it automatically.
  • Don't count on a queue: MDN is explicit that some screen readers read several announcements in a row, but it's not guaranteed and often only the latest one is spoken. If you have two things to say, say them in a single call.
  • Live regions still win: per MDN, aria-live announcements take priority over ariaNotify() ones. If you mix both, the live region goes first.
  • macOS and ChromeOS: MDN's compatibility data notes that with VoiceOver an announcement may be dropped if another accessibility event fires at the same moment, and that on ChromeOS the method exists in Chrome but announcements are never spoken.
  • Iframes: usage is controlled by the aria-notify permissions policy. Its default allowlist is *, so it works inside iframes unless someone blocks it, and when it is blocked the announcements fail silently.
  • Don't spam: not needing user activation is convenient, but every announcement interrupts someone who is listening. One message per relevant event, short and useful.

What to keep an eye on

  • How each screen reader handles the queue and high priority. This is where behaviour will vary most for a while, so it's worth testing with NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver rather than trusting the simulation.
  • When the share of browsers without support is small enough to drop the live region fallback in your project.
  • The spec only defines normal and high for now. If more options are added, they will show up in the AriaNotificationOptions dictionary.

Sources

  • Element: ariaNotify() method, MDN
  • Document: ariaNotify() method, MDN
  • Interface Mixin ARIANotifyMixin, WAI-ARIA (W3C Editor's Draft)
  • Chrome 141 beta, Chrome for Developers
  • ariaNotify(), Web Platform Status
