articles.title: React 20 Compiler: Which Hooks It Eliminates, Which It Cannot, and How to Audit Your Codebase Before Upgrading
articles.description: The React Compiler auto-memoizes components and hooks, eliminating most useMemo and useCallback calls. Developers must audit effect dependencies, library compatibility, and exact-identity patterns before migrating.
articles.body_html:
React 20 Compiler: Which Hooks It Eliminates, Which It Cannot, and How to Audit Your Codebase Before Upgrading

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

The React Compiler shipped with React 19 as a stable Babel plugin that automatically memoizes components and hooks, eliminating the majority of manual useMemo, useCallback, and React.memo calls. Teams installing version 1.0.0 today find that most performance-oriented memoization becomes redundant. The compiler analyzes data flow, understands mutability, and applies granular memoization that survives conditional returns and early exits where manual hooks fail.

The problem surfaces when developers treat the compiler as a drop-in replacement without auditing the semantic contracts their existing hooks enforce. A useCallback wrapping an event handler for performance looks identical in the source to one ensuring exact reference identity for a useEffect dependency array. The compiler sees both as memoization candidates, removes them, and breaks the second use case. The codebase compiles, tests pass in isolation, and production deploys a useEffect that fires on every render because the dependency lost its stable identity.

The solution requires a three-phase audit before enabling the compiler: running the ESLint plugin to surface Rules of React violations, checking library compatibility for interior mutability patterns, and marking effect-dependency memoization with explicit comments or redesigning the dependency contracts. Developers who complete this audit can enable the compiler with confidence, knowing which hooks to keep and which the compiler handles transparently.

Key Takeaways

  • The React Compiler automatically memoizes components and hooks, making most useMemo, useCallback, and React.memo calls redundant for performance-only use cases.
  • Effect dependencies relying on exact identity require explicit useMemo or a redesigned dependency contract before compiler migration.
  • Libraries with interior mutability (React Hook Form, TanStack Table, MobX) need per-component "use no memo" directives or wrapper patterns.
  • The ESLint plugin in eslint-plugin-react-hooks@latest identifies Rules of React violations without requiring compiler installation, serving as the first migration audit step.
  • Pin the compiler to an exact version (--save-exact) if test coverage is incomplete to prevent unexpected memoization changes across minor releases.

Which Hooks the React Compiler Eliminates (and the Patterns It Auto-Memoizes)

The compiler targets memoization hooks installed solely for performance optimization. Any useMemo or useCallback wrapping an expensive computation, JSX generation, or event handler receives automatic granular memoization that the compiler derives from its static analysis. The official documentation confirms the compiler handles memoization automatically, including cases where manual hooks cannot be placed, such as after an early return.

A component that filters a large dataset and renders a virtualized list no longer needs explicit useMemo around the filter operation. The compiler detects the data dependency, memoizes the filtered result, and re-computes only when the source array or filter predicate changes. The same applies to event handlers wrapped in useCallback to prevent child re-renders. The compiler memoizes the handler automatically and propagates reference stability where it matters.

The compiler also memoizes conditionally, a pattern impossible with manual hooks. A component that returns null early based on a prop check can still have its post-return JSX memoized because the compiler understands the control flow and applies memoization to the reachable paths.

export default function ProductCard({ product }) {
  if (!product) {
    return null;
  }

  // Compiler memoizes this computation after the early return
  const discountedPrice = product.price * (1 - product.discount);

  return (
    <div className="card">
      <h3>{product.name}</h3>
      <p className="price">${discountedPrice.toFixed(2)}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

The React 19 release announcement states the compiler supports optional chains and array indices as dependencies, improving the precision of automatic memoization and reducing over-memoization in components that previously required manual hooks to avoid unnecessary re-renders.

React Compiler automatic memoization visualization

Which Hooks and Patterns the Compiler Cannot Handle

The compiler cannot remove hooks that enforce semantic contracts beyond performance. Effect dependencies requiring exact identity guarantees, libraries with interior mutability, and escape hatches for explicit control over memoization granularity remain manual responsibilities.

Effect dependencies represent the most common compiler limitation. A useMemo wrapping a configuration object passed to a useEffect dependency array ensures the effect fires only when the configuration semantically changes, not when the parent component re-renders. The compiler sees the object creation, memoizes it for performance, but does not understand the identity contract the effect requires.

function DataFetcher({ userId, filters }) {
  // This useMemo must stay: the effect needs exact identity
  const queryConfig = useMemo(
    () => ({ userId, filters, timestamp: Date.now() }),
    [userId, filters]
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch(`/api/data?${new URLSearchParams(queryConfig)}`);
  }, [queryConfig]); // Effect fires only when userId/filters change
}

Libraries with interior mutability break the compiler's assumption that props and state are immutable. React Hook Form's watch() method, TanStack Table's row model, and MobX observables all mutate internal state without triggering React's normal render cycle. The compiler cannot track these mutations and may apply memoization that prevents the component from seeing updates.

Third-party hooks that violate the Rules of React also bypass compiler optimization. A custom hook calling another hook conditionally or in a loop receives a compilation error or silent skipping, leaving the component unmemoized.

Pattern Compiler behavior Developer action
Effect dependency identity Memoizes for performance, not identity Keep explicit useMemo or redesign dependency
Interior mutability (RHF, TanStack, MobX) May prevent component updates Add "use no memo" directive or wrapper
Conditional hook calls Skips compilation with error Fix Rules of React violation before enabling
Expensive computation with no identity contract Auto-memoizes Remove manual useMemo

Pre-Migration Audit: Running the ESLint Plugin and Identifying Manual Optimization Debt

The first migration step runs the ESLint plugin from eslint-plugin-react-hooks@latest to surface Rules of React violations before the compiler touches production code. The React Compiler documentation recommends installing the plugin standalone, without the compiler, because it identifies breaking patterns that will cause silent compilation failures.

The plugin flags setState patterns that cause render loops, expensive work inside effects, and unsafe ref access during render. These violations break the compiler's data-flow assumptions and must be fixed before enabling automatic memoization.

npm install --save-dev eslint-plugin-react-hooks@latest

// eslint.config.js (Flat Config)
import reactHooks from 'eslint-plugin-react-hooks';
import { defineConfig } from 'eslint/config';

export default defineConfig([
  reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended,
]);

The second audit step catalogs every useMemo and useCallback in the codebase and classifies each by intent. Performance-only hooks receive a // Performance: compiler handles comment and a ticket to remove them in the next cleanup sprint. Identity-contract hooks receive a // Identity contract: keep for effect dependency comment and remain in the codebase permanently.

A spreadsheet tracking hook location, intent, and removal status provides visibility into the migration. Teams with thousands of memoization hooks prioritize high-traffic components first and leave low-risk utilities for later sprints.

Library Compatibility Check: React Hook Form, TanStack, MobX, and Interior Mutability

Libraries relying on interior mutability require component-level compiler opt-outs or wrapper patterns that isolate the mutability from compiled code. The compiler's auto-memoization assumes props and state are immutable and that re-renders propagate through standard React update mechanisms. Libraries violating these assumptions need explicit handling.

React Hook Form's watch() method mutates internal subscription state without triggering React updates. A component calling watch('fieldName') directly in the render body and relying on the compiler for memoization will not see field value changes because the compiler's memoization cache does not invalidate when the form's internal state changes.

The community discussion on React Hook Form compatibility identifies three patterns that survive the compiler: passing primitives to child components instead of the entire form object, having children call useFormState directly, and binding fields with <Controller> or useController whenever the value is rewritten programmatically through reset() or useForm({ values }). Plain register does not survive React Hook Form's internal _reset under the compiler because the reset mechanism bypasses the compiler's dependency tracking.

TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual present similar challenges. The row model from useReactTable() is a mutable object that updates in place. Components extracting rows and mapping them to JSX need a "use no memo" directive at the component level or a wrapper component that calls the hook and passes primitives down.

'use no memo';

export function DataTable({ columns, data }) {
  const table = useReactTable({
    data,
    columns,
    getCoreRowModel: getCoreRowModel(),
  });

  return (
    <table>
      <tbody>
        {table.getRowModel().rows.map(row => (
          <tr key={row.id}>
            {row.getVisibleCells().map(cell => (
              <td key={cell.id}>
                {flexRender(cell.column.columnDef.cell, cell.getContext())}
              </td>
            ))}
          </tr>
        ))}
      </tbody>
    </table>
  );
}
Library Mutability pattern Compiler compatibility Recommended action
React Hook Form watch() mutates subscriptions Breaks without wrappers Use Controller, useFormState, or pass primitives
TanStack Table Row model mutates in place Breaks without opt-out Add "use no memo" or wrapper component
TanStack Virtual Virtualizer mutates scroll state Breaks without opt-out Add "use no memo" or wrapper component
MobX Observables mutate without React updates Breaks without observer Keep MobX observer wrapper
Immer Draft state mutates during produce Compatible Compiler understands Immer's immutability contract

MobX requires the observer higher-order component to track observable access and trigger re-renders. The compiler does not interfere with MobX's reactivity system, but teams using MobX should keep the observer wrapper and avoid relying on the compiler to memoize components that read observables.

Code Examples: When to Keep useMemo for Effect Dependencies and Exact Identity

Effect dependencies requiring exact identity represent the clearest case for keeping explicit useMemo. The compiler's automatic memoization optimizes for performance, not identity contracts. A useEffect that fetches data when a query configuration changes needs the configuration object to maintain the same reference across renders unless the underlying values change.

function SearchResults({ query, filters, sortBy }) {
  // Keep this useMemo: the effect needs exact identity
  const searchConfig = useMemo(
    () => ({
      query,
      filters,
      sortBy,
      includeArchived: false,
    }),
    [query, filters, sortBy]
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();

    fetch('/api/search', {
      method: 'POST',
      body: JSON.stringify(searchConfig),
      signal: controller.signal,
    })
      .then(res => res.json())
      .then(setResults);

    return () => controller.abort();
  }, [searchConfig]); // Effect fires only when config semantically changes

  return <ResultsList results={results} />;
}

The alternative pattern flattens the dependency array and removes the object wrapper, making the identity contract explicit in the effect itself.

function SearchResults({ query, filters, sortBy }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();

    // No useMemo needed: dependencies are primitives
    fetch('/api/search', {
      method: 'POST',
      body: JSON.stringify({
        query,
        filters,
        sortBy,
        includeArchived: false,
      }),
      signal: controller.signal,
    })
      .then(res => res.json())
      .then(setResults);

    return () => controller.abort();
  }, [query, filters, sortBy]); // Effect tracks primitives directly

  return <ResultsList results={results} />;
}

The second pattern eliminates the useMemo by removing the object from the dependency array entirely. The compiler handles the fetch call's memoization automatically, and the effect dependency array contains only primitives that React compares by value.

Effect dependency identity contract visualization

The decision between keeping useMemo and refactoring the dependency array depends on the team's tolerance for dependency-array length and the semantic clarity of the object wrapper. Configurations with six or more fields benefit from the object wrapper because the dependency array becomes unreadable. Configurations with two or three fields flatten easily.

Related patterns appear in event handlers passed to third-party libraries that compare handler references to optimize internal subscriptions. A charting library that subscribes to a onDataPointClick callback and unsubscribes on reference change needs the handler wrapped in useCallback to prevent subscription churn.

function InteractiveChart({ data }) {
  // Keep this useCallback: the library checks reference equality
  const handleDataPointClick = useCallback((point) => {
    analytics.track('chart_interaction', { pointId: point.id });
  }, []); // Empty deps: handler never changes

  return (
    <Chart
      data={data}
      onDataPointClick={handleDataPointClick}
    />
  );
}

The compiler will memoize the handler automatically, but the explicit useCallback documents the identity contract for future maintainers. Removing it saves three lines of code at the cost of losing the semantic signal that the library depends on reference stability.

For additional context on managing state and effects in modern React applications, see our guides on building apps with just React hooks and atomic state management with Jotai.

Phase-by-Phase Migration Strategy: Installing, Testing, and Removing Hooks Safely

A safe migration starts with installing the compiler in a single low-risk component tree, validating behavior in production, and expanding coverage incrementally. The React Compiler documentation provides gating strategies, compatibility checks, and rollout tooling for gradual adoption.

Phase one installs the compiler and runs the ESLint plugin on the entire codebase. Developers fix Rules of React violations flagged by the plugin before enabling the compiler anywhere.

npm install --save-dev --save-exact babel-plugin-react-compiler@latest
npm install --save-dev eslint-plugin-react-hooks@latest

Phase two enables the compiler for a single component tree in production and monitors render count, interaction latency, and error rate metrics for regressions. A low-risk tree contains no third-party library integrations, no complex effect dependencies, and no performance-critical paths that would make debugging difficult.

Phase three expands compiler coverage to the next component tree after confirming the first tree's metrics remain stable for a week. Teams with insufficient test coverage pin the compiler to an exact version using --save-exact to prevent SemVer updates from changing memoization behavior between deployments.

npm install --save-dev --save-exact babel-plugin-react-compiler@1.0.0

The compiler documentation warns that future versions may change how memoization is applied, becoming more granular and precise. These changes optimize performance but can cause unexpected behavior in codebases that break the Rules of React in ways JavaScript cannot statically detect. Continuous end-to-end testing and exact version pinning mitigate this risk.

Phase four removes manual useMemo and useCallback hooks marked as performance-only during the audit. Developers submit small pull requests removing five to ten hooks at a time, run the test suite, and merge after confirming no behavioral changes. Identity-contract hooks remain permanently with comments explaining the contract.

function DataGrid({ rows, columns, onRowClick }) {
  // Identity contract: keep for effect dependency and third-party library
  const gridConfig = useMemo(
    () => ({ rows, columns, virtualizer: true }),
    [rows, columns]
  );

  // Performance: compiler handles (remove this hook)
  // const sortedRows = useMemo(() => rows.sort(compareRows), [rows]);

  return <VirtualizedTable config={gridConfig} onClick={onRowClick} />;
}

Phase five audits library compatibility and adds "use no memo" directives to components using React Hook Form, TanStack, or MobX. These directives prevent the compiler from memoizing the component, preserving the library's interior mutability behavior.

For teams building accessible forms, our guide on useFormStatus and useFormState demonstrates patterns that work seamlessly with the compiler.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can the React Compiler break production if enabled globally without testing?

Yes. The compiler changes how memoization is applied and may expose latent bugs in code that violates the Rules of React. Effect dependencies relying on exact identity, libraries with interior mutability, and components with conditional hook calls will produce unexpected behavior. Enable the compiler incrementally, starting with low-risk component trees and monitoring production metrics.

Do I need to remove all useMemo and useCallback hooks immediately after installing the compiler?

No. The compiler works correctly with existing memoization hooks in place. Remove hooks incrementally after confirming they serve performance-only purposes. Keep hooks that enforce identity contracts for effect dependencies or third-party library requirements. Removing all hooks at once increases the risk of missing semantic contracts.

Which version of React do I need to use the compiler?

The compiler supports React 17 and up. Teams on React 17 or 18 must specify a minimum target in the compiler config and add react-compiler-runtime as a dependency. React 19 includes native compiler support without additional runtime dependencies.

How do I know if a third-party library is compatible with the compiler?

Check the library's documentation for compiler compatibility notes. Libraries with interior mutability (React Hook Form, TanStack Table, MobX) require component-level opt-outs or wrapper patterns. Run the ESLint plugin to identify Rules violations in library integration code. When unsure, add a "use no memo" directive to the component and test behavior before and after.

What happens if the compiler skips a component due to a Rules violation?

The compiler silently skips components that violate the Rules of React and does not apply automatic memoization. The component continues to work but receives no performance optimization. The ESLint plugin from eslint-plugin-react-hooks@latest flags these violations during development, allowing developers to fix them before deployment.

Conclusion

The React Compiler eliminates manual memoization for performance but leaves developers responsible for identity contracts, library compatibility, and Rules of React compliance. Teams running the ESLint audit first, cataloging effect dependencies second, and enabling the compiler incrementally gain performance improvements without breaking production. Every useMemo that remains after migration should document the specific identity contract or library requirement it enforces. The compiler handles the rest.

articles.title: How I rank 250 countries for every month of the year
articles.description: Two penalties, 30 years of climate data and one Postgres query build twelve monthly rankings. Here's how it works, and which assumption matters most.
articles.body_html:
PickOH, the travel site I run, has twelve ranking pages, one per month. Where to Go in August currently lists 62 countries and territories, from Malawi at #1 to Svalbard at #62. Nobody orders them by hand. A scoring formula and one Postgres query build all twelve pages from 30 years of climate data.

This post covers how the ranking works, the bug that gave four countries the same #1, and what happened when each assumption in the formula was tested.

The data: one point per country, 30 years deep

Each of the 250 countries and territories has twelve rows in Postgres, one per month: average daily high, average daily low, total rainfall and rain days. The numbers are 1991–2020 climate normals from the ERA5 reanalysis, fetched through Open-Meteo's archive API. Each one is measured at a single location, usually the capital.

Fetching it mostly took patience: 30-year requests use up Open-Meteo's free quota quickly, so the backfill had to cache and resume per location. Auditing the result was the harder job:

  • Ten places, including Finland, Iceland and Russia, shared one identical placeholder temperature curve that peaked in April.
  • Sixteen large countries stored temperatures from the wrong region: the Sahara for Algeria, the Andes for Peru, the outback for Australia, Mumbai for India. Their rainfall and coordinates described the capital, so each row was describing two places at once.
  • Checking every remaining location against ERA5 found 32 more like that.

The fix came down to one rule: temperature, rain and coordinates must all describe the same place. Bolivia stayed as it was, because ERA5 misreads the sharp relief around La Paz and the stored curve already matched the real city.

The score

Every month of every country gets a penalty score. Lower is better, and 0 is a perfect month.

The temperature penalty is the number of degrees the average daily high sits outside 18–26°C. The rain penalty treats 25 mm of monthly rain as one degree of discomfort. A month at 30°C with 50 mm of rain scores 4 + 2 = 6.

A country's two lowest-scoring months become its picks. Exact ties go to the drier month, then the earlier one.

Why two? Jordan is a good example:

Amman is cool and damp in winter, then dry but hitting 33–36°C in summer. The good months sit between those seasons, so the picks land in October and April. A single best month would hide one of them.

That shape is common. 64 of the 250 have picks that aren't consecutive months, and for 10 of them, including China, the two picks are exactly six months apart.

Temperature alone wouldn't be enough. 135 countries have three or more months inside the band, which would leave those months tied at zero. Colombia is the extreme case: Bogotá's average high stays between 18 and 20°C all year, so rain alone picks August and September.

Two stages, not one sort

The obvious design is to sort all 250 by each month's score. The pages do something different:

  1. Qualify. A country appears on a month's page only if that month is one of its own two picks. This compares a country with itself.
  2. Order. The qualifiers are sorted by raw score. This compares countries with each other.

So August's page means "places at their best in August", not "the mildest places on Earth in August". A plain sort answers the second question, and the answer barely changes: Saint Helena would make the top ten in 11 months of the year, and every page would be 250 entries long.

Because qualifying is relative, places that are never pleasant still get two months. 92 of the 250 never have a month inside the band. Iceland peaks at 14.5°C in July, and both of Antarctica's best months are below freezing. Stage two handles them: Iceland is #52 of 60 for July, and Antarctica is #41 of 41 for December.

Both stages run in a single Postgres query per page. The same query finds each country's other pick, which becomes the "Also great in July" line on its card.

The bug: four countries at #1

The page position originally used competition ranking, where tied entries share a number. Malawi, Peru, Zambia and Zimbabwe all round to a score of 0.0 for August, so the cards read #1, #1, #1, #1, #5. The database was doing exactly what it was asked to do, and the page still looked broken.

Switching to a simple running count over the same order fixed it. The rounding stayed, so countries with effectively identical weather fall alphabetically instead of being separated by differences no traveller would notice.

One formula, three copies

Each country's Weather tab shows the same picks, with the two months marked in gold and green:

That creates a maintenance problem, because the scoring logic exists in three places:

  • TypeScript in the browser, for those Weather tab badges
  • SQL, for the month pages
  • TypeScript on the server, for the best-month text in server-rendered HTML

Comments say to change them together, and a unit test pins the key parts of the query. Neither proves they agree. So for this post, an independent Python version of the score was run on every country's twelve months from the live API and compared with all twelve ranking pages: 250 countries, 500 picks, 0 mismatches.

That check isn't in CI, which is the weak spot. A shared fixture that all three implementations have to pass would close it.

Which assumption matters most?

The 25 mm constant and the 18–26°C band are both judgement calls. To see how much each one matters, the picks were recalculated with different values, counting how many countries' top month changed:

The rain constant is stable. Moving it to 20 or 30 mm changes 2–3% of top picks, and doubling or halving it changes 7–11%. Removing rain altogether changes 21%, even with the drier month still winning ties.

The comfort band is the strongest opinion in the model. Sliding it 2°C either way changes 22–24% of top picks, and stretching the top to 30°C changes 29%. Someone planning a beach holiday would want a warmer band and would get a noticeably different list. The band is already a parameter, so a personal comfort setting wouldn't need new scoring logic.

The year isn't evenly spread

Each country gets two picks, but they don't land evenly across the calendar:

The February and August peaks come mostly from the tropics, where the dry season flips across the equator. In January and February, 89 of the 90 tropical picks come from north of the equator. By July and August, 52 of 71 come from south of it. Countries north of the tropics cluster around May and September, either side of the summer heat.

What the score can't see

  • Cloud. Peru is #2 for August: 21°C and under 1 mm of rain in Lima. The score is nearly perfect, but Lima's winter is known for grey skies and garúa, a coastal mist that barely registers as rain.
  • Humidity. Only the daily high counts, so a sticky 30°C scores the same as a dry one. Night lows and rain days appear on the cards but aren't scored.
  • Geography. One point stands in for a whole country. China's picks are Beijing's, which says nothing about tropical Hainan.
  • Grid resolution. ERA5 uses a 0.25° grid, roughly 25 km. Tokyo's stored August high is 27°C, while published climate tables put it near 30°C. At 30°C, August would drop out of Japan's top two and April would replace it.
  • Good months that miss the cut. Greece's October scores 1.10, which would place it around #7 on October's page, but it isn't listed because May and September score better. Across the year, 193 of the 408 country-months scoring 2 or better don't appear on any page. It's also why page length says little about how many good options exist: November lists 17 countries while 31 score that well, and July lists 60 while only 23 do.

The ranking has to exist in the HTML too

The month pages are React, and the browser fetches the ranking after load. Early on, curl on a month page found zero <a href> tags, so anything that didn't run JavaScript saw no ranking and no links.

The server now loads the same ranking and renders it as plain anchors in the initial HTML. Between them, the twelve pages link every country's weather page. Three details matter:

  • The server-rendered list has to match what the page shows, in the same order. Anything else is cloaking.
  • If the query fails, the page still renders without its links rather than returning an error.
  • The bare /where-to-go URL answers with a 302 and Cache-Control: no-store, because its target changes every month.

All twelve months

Here is every page, with the number of countries that qualify:

January (50) · February (65) · March (28) · April (24) · May (44) · June (36) · July (60) · August (62) · September (45) · October (28) · November (17) · December (41)

If you were adding one more term to the score, would it be cloud cover or humidity? I'd like to hear how you'd weight it.

articles.title: Turning a video clip into a game sprite sheet in the browser
articles.description: I make 2D characters by generating a short animation video and cutting it into a sprite sheet. For a...
articles.body_html:
I make 2D characters by generating a short animation video and cutting it into a sprite sheet. For a while that meant ffmpeg, a Python script and a lot of fiddling with transparency. I moved the whole thing into a browser page so it runs on the user's machine and the video never leaves it. This post is what I learned along the way: reading frames from a <video>, removing a flat backdrop from compressed frames, and keeping the character's feet in place.


A character reference turned into an animated sprite (AI-generated with SpriteCanvas)

All code below is plain JavaScript with no dependencies.

1. Reading frames: seek, wait, draw

There is no "give me frame 37" API on HTMLVideoElement. What works everywhere is: set currentTime, wait for seeked, draw the video to a canvas, read the pixels.

// Call after the video fired 'loadeddata', so the first frame is decoded.
async function readFrames(video, times, width, height) {
  const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
  canvas.width = width;
  canvas.height = height;
  const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d', { willReadFrequently: true });
  const frames = [];
  for (const t of times) {
    if (Math.abs(video.currentTime - t) > 0.001) {
      const seeked = new Promise((resolve) => video.addEventListener('seeked', resolve, { once: true }));
      video.currentTime = t;
      await seeked;
    }
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, width, height);
    ctx.drawImage(video, 0, 0, width, height);
    frames.push(ctx.getImageData(0, 0, width, height).data);
  }
  return frames;
}

Three things bit me:

  • Don't seek to the very end. A seek to exactly video.duration often shows no frame. I keep every sample time below duration - 0.01.
  • Round the sample times. start + i / fps accumulates float error; I round to microseconds so 0.1 + 0.2 style noise doesn't skip or duplicate a frame.
  • Background tabs stall. Chrome holds back video loading and decoding in a hidden tab, so a long read just stops when the user switches tabs. Before every seek I wait until the tab is visible again: 
function whenVisible() {
  if (!document.hidden) return Promise.resolve();
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    const shown = () => {
      if (document.hidden) return;
      document.removeEventListener('visibilitychange', shown);
      resolve();
    };
    document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', shown);
  });
}

I also cap the read at 512 frames and check frames × width × height × 4 bytes up front, because a 10-second 1080p clip at 30 fps is about 2.5 GB of RGBA.

requestVideoFrameCallback and WebCodecs are faster, but the first follows playback and drops frames when the page is busy, and the second needs its own demuxer. Seeking is the one path that behaves the same in Chrome, Firefox and Safari, and for a few hundred frames it is fast enough.

2. Finding the backdrop

Generated clips and green-screen recordings have a flat backdrop, so I look at the four corners. For PNG sheets I require the corners to match within 12 per channel. Video frames carry compression noise, so there I allow 24 and use the average of the corners as the key colour.

function detectBackdrop(rgba, w, h) {
  const corners = [0, (w - 1) * 4, (h - 1) * w * 4, ((h - 1) * w + w - 1) * 4];
  const first = corners[0];
  const close = (p) => [0, 1, 2].every((c) => Math.abs(rgba[p + c] - rgba[first + c]) <= 24);
  if (!corners.every(close)) return null;
  return [0, 1, 2].map((c) => Math.round(corners.reduce((sum, p) => sum + rgba[p + c], 0) / 4));
}

3. Removing it: flood fill vs. "everywhere"

For a still sprite sheet I flood-fill from the edges, so a backdrop-coloured pixel inside the character (a green gem on a green screen) survives. For video I clear every matching pixel, like a chroma key, because the gaps between arms and legs are not connected to the border in every frame, and a flood fill leaves them filled.

The hard part is the edge. A scaled, compressed video leaves a one-pixel ring of blended colour around the character: half character, half magenta. Clearing by a tolerance either leaves a pink halo or eats into the character.

What worked: for each remaining pixel that touches a cleared pixel, compare it with the pixel just inside it, the neighbour on the opposite side from the cleared one. If it sits more than halfway from that inner pixel towards the backdrop colour, it is fringe and goes. When the inner pixel is cleared too, the pixel is part of a one-pixel line, so I keep it.

// How far p is from the inner pixel q towards the backdrop colour: 0 at q, 1 at the backdrop.
function towardBackdrop(rgba, p, q, key) {
  let dot = 0, len = 0;
  for (let c = 0; c < 3; c++) {
    const axis = key[c] - rgba[q + c];
    dot += (rgba[p + c] - rgba[q + c]) * axis;
    len += axis * axis;
  }
  return len ? dot / len : 1;
}

This is a projection onto the line between the sprite colour and the key colour, so it works for any backdrop colour and any character colour, without a per-video tolerance.

4. Trimming without losing the motion

Each video frame is mostly empty, so I crop. The trap: cropping each frame to its own bounding box makes the character jump around, because a sword swing makes the box wider in some frames. Crop every frame by the union of all the boxes instead; relative motion stays intact and the sheet is still small.

const union = boxes.reduce((u, b) => !b ? u : !u ? b : {
  x0: Math.min(u.x0, b.x0), y0: Math.min(u.y0, b.y0),
  x1: Math.max(u.x1, b.x1), y1: Math.max(u.y1, b.y1),
}, null);

There is an optional second step for clips where the camera drifts: move each frame so the bottom centre of its content lands where the first frame's does. I leave it off by default, because for a jump the feet are supposed to leave the ground.

5. The atlas

The output is one PNG in a grid plus a JSON Hash atlas, which Phaser and PixiJS load as is. Two fields matter beyond the frame rectangles:

"frames": {
  "hero-attack-03": {
    "frame": { "x": 768, "y": 0, "w": 256, "h": 256 },
    "pivot": { "x": 0.5, "y": 0.875 },
    "duration": 83
  }
}
  • pivot is the foot point, so every animation of a character stands on the same line in the engine.
  • duration is per frame in milliseconds. Phaser keeps unknown frame fields in customData and ignores duration for playback, so pass it yourself: 
const tex = this.textures.get('hero-attack');
this.anims.create({
  key: 'attack',
  frames: tex.getFrameNames().sort().map((frame) => ({
    key: 'hero-attack', frame, duration: tex.get(frame).customData?.duration,
  })),
});

(getFrameNames() has no guaranteed order; zero-padded names make .sort() enough. This is for Phaser 3.80 and later, where a frame's duration replaces the base frame time; up to 3.70 it is added on top.)

What I'd do differently

  • Ask for a flat, unusual backdrop colour (magenta) when generating the clip. Green screen fights green cloaks.
  • Ask for the last frame to match the first. Loops stop popping, and you don't have to hunt for a loop point.
  • A "breathing" idle that is just the sprite scaled up and down looks fake in the engine. Generate a real idle motion (chest, shoulders, cloth) instead. I shipped the scaled kind first and had to redo it.

The tool from this post is free and runs in the browser: video to sprite sheet. I built it as part of SpriteCanvas, which also generates the character and the animation clips; the sample art here was made with it (AI-generated).

articles.title: Building a free AI UI builder on Cloudflare: what small models taught me
articles.description: A 2 days ago I launched openconstructor, a free, open-source browser editor: you describe an...
articles.body_html:
A 2 days ago I launched openconstructor, a free, open-source browser editor: you describe an interface, an AI builds it on a canvas, and you keep editing by hand or ask the AI to change one part. It got 562 visitors in its first two days with no ads.

The whole thing runs on a Cloudflare Worker, Supabase and free open models. Here are the parts that turned out more interesting than I expected.

1. Small free models can't design, so I stopped asking them to

The built-in AI runs on open models (GPT-OSS 120B, Llama 3.3 70B) through Workers AI. They write valid HTML, but ask for an "award-winning cinematic website" and you get something different every time: sometimes great, often a plain hero and three cards.

Prompt engineering got me maybe 20% further. What worked was splitting the job:

  • the design is a set of hand-made sections (hero with a CSS 3D object, scroll-lit statement, services, case studies, logo wall…);
  • the model only writes the content, as JSON. 
// the model gets a schema with defaults and returns only this
{
  "brand": "Ember", "hue": 28,
  "titleA": "Roasted by fire.", "titleB": "Poured with care.",
  "services": [["Roast", "Small batches on a 1960s drum roaster."], ...],
  "heroArt": "amber neon cube over dark sand dunes, cinematic 3d render"
}

The page is then assembled from the sections. hue rotates the template's accent colours, so a coffee roaster gets amber and an AI lab gets violet. Same model, but the result went from "sometimes nice" to consistently polished, in about 6 seconds.

Lesson: with weak models, move the taste into code and let the model fill in the blanks.

2. Published pages run zero JavaScript

Users publish pages to openconstructor.pw/p/<name>. Since anyone can publish, every page is served with:

Content-Security-Policy: sandbox allow-forms ...; script-src 'none'

No scripts at all. So how do pages still feel alive? Modern CSS covers more than I thought:

@supports (animation-timeline: view()) {
  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
    .section {
      animation: rise linear both;
      animation-timeline: view();
      animation-range: entry 0% cover 30%;
    }
  }
}
@keyframes rise { from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(64px); } }

Scroll-driven animations, perspective + preserve-3d for floating 3D objects, marquees with mask fades: all without a single line of JS. Browsers without support just show the content.

3. Screenshots without a server

The sandbox has a side effect: the page has an opaque origin, so the gallery can't measure or screenshot it in an iframe. Headless Chrome on the server would be costly.

Instead, the editor takes the screenshot itself at publish time:

  1. lay the page out in a hidden iframe to measure its height;
  2. put the HTML into an SVG <foreignObject>;
  3. draw that SVG onto a <canvas> and export JPEG. 
const svg = `<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="${w}" height="${h}">
  <foreignObject width="100%" height="100%">${xhtml}</foreignObject></svg>`;
img.src = 'data:image/svg+xml,' + encodeURIComponent(svg);
ctx.drawImage(img, 0, 0);
canvas.toBlob(upload, 'image/jpeg', 0.82);

The worker stores two images in KV: a 1200×630 one for link previews (og:image) and a full-page one for the gallery, which scrolls through it on hover. About 40 KB each.

4. My biggest mistake: a sign-up wall I didn't notice

After launch I looked at the numbers: hundreds of visitors, two accounts. It turned out the free AI required signing in. So most people opened the editor, typed a prompt and hit a login form.

Now visitors get 3 free generations a day without an account (counted in KV per hashed IP, the IP itself isn't stored). An account gives 20 a day, cloud projects and publishing. A friendly offer appears after the first good result, not before.

Lesson: test your product signed out, in a private window, before every launch post.

Try it / read the code

  • Live: https://openconstructor.pw
  • Code: https://github.com/Kuloka/openconstructor

It also exports to React, Vue, Svelte and even Roblox UI and LÖVE 2D. I'd love feedback, especially on where the AI output falls apart.

articles.title: How I Handle Ambiguous API Timeouts in an AI Video App
articles.description: A video-generation request times out. There is no task ID in the response. Should the application...
articles.body_html:
A video-generation request times out. There is no task ID in the response. Should the application send it again?

The awkward answer is that the provider might already be generating the video. The response could have disappeared after the task was accepted. Sending the same payload again could start another paid task.

I built I Love the Smiths AI, a small photo-to-video app that turns one or two photos into a 20-second elevator scene. The user-facing flow is short. Behind it, I need to distinguish between a failed generation and a request whose outcome I simply do not know.

This is how the job-processing code handles that distinction.

Two kinds of duplicate request

The first duplicate comes from the browser. A user clicks again, refreshes, or loses the response from my server.

Each generation carries a request ID. The server uses that ID as the job's primary key. When it receives an existing ID, it checks that the owner and serialized input match the original request. A matching request returns the existing job; a changed input or different owner is rejected.

That check matters. Reusing an ID cannot quietly turn a request for one person's photos into a request for someone else's.

Job creation also debits the user's video allowance through a database trigger. The insertion and debit belong to the same database operation. If the allowance cannot be spent, the job insertion rolls back. A duplicate insertion does not spend another allowance.

The second duplicate is harder: submitting the job to the external video service twice. My database can recognize a repeated browser request. That alone cannot deduplicate work inside another system.

Record the submission attempt before making the call

Before calling the provider, the worker persists a submission timestamp. That update is conditional: the job must still be queued, the worker must hold the current claim, and there must be no earlier submission marker.

If the call returns a task ID, the worker saves it and moves the job into processing. Later attempts can ask about that specific task instead of creating another one.

If the response is lost, the record is different: the submission marker exists, but the provider task ID is missing. The code leaves the allowance reserved and exposes a support-review message. It does not automatically submit again.

These are the recovery decisions, reduced to a table:

What the application knows Next action
No submission marker or provider task ID Claim the job, record the attempt, then submit
A provider task ID exists Check that task's status
A submission marker exists without a task ID Hold for reconciliation; do not create another task
The provider definitely rejected the request Record failure and restore the allowance

There is a cost to recording the marker first. A worker could stop after writing it but before sending the request. That job would also need review, even though no provider task was created.

I accept that uncertainty in this integration. It avoids automatically turning an unknown result into another billable submission. The marker is a guard against automatic resubmission, not proof that the provider accepted anything.

A lease needs a claim number

More than one execution can reach a pending job. A scheduled reconciliation pass may overlap another execution, and a slow network operation can outlive the worker's lease.

The worker therefore claims a job through a conditional database update. Each successful claim increments an attempt counter. Subsequent writes must match that counter and an unexpired lease.

The condition has this shape, with names shortened for clarity:

UPDATE video_job
SET status = ?, updated_at = ?
WHERE id = ?
  AND attempts = ?
  AND lease_until > ?
  AND status IN ('queued', 'processing', 'composing', 'saving')
RETURNING *;

Suppose worker A has claim 4 and waits on a response. Its lease expires. Worker B takes over and gets claim 5. When A eventually receives its response, its claim-4 update cannot overwrite B's work.

Checking only a timestamp would be insufficient: A might observe that the job now has a valid lease, but that lease belongs to B. The claim number identifies which execution owns the write.

This protects local state. It does not cancel an external request that is already in flight, which is why the submission marker is a separate concern.

Saving the file is another recoverable step

The provider finishing a video is not the end of the job. The application still needs to fetch, validate, and store the result.

The code records the provider's result URL before starting that copy. On a later processing attempt, an existing result URL sends the job back into the saving step. A storage failure therefore does not require another model-generation request.

Output object keys also include the claim number. An old worker finishing an upload late cannot overwrite the object uploaded by a newer claim. Publishing the saved file as the job's result still requires the guarded database update.

That separation is useful because a network failure while copying bytes says nothing about whether the model generated the scene successfully.

Failure and uncertainty have different accounting

A confirmed provider failure, a definite submission rejection, or an invalid generated video can move the job to failed. A database trigger restores the video allowance using a unique refund reference, so the transition cannot repeatedly credit the same job.

An ambiguous submission does not take that path. Its allowance stays reserved while the outcome is unresolved. Here, restoring an allowance means returning a generation use to the order; it is separate from issuing a payment refund.

The regression cases in the repository include concurrent duplicate requests, an unknown submission that must not be recreated, stale worker responses, and a storage failure that resumes from the recorded result. Those cases describe the boundaries I want the implementation to preserve.

The remaining compromise is manual reconciliation when submission acknowledgement is lost. A provider-supported idempotency key or reliable lookup by client request ID could improve that recovery path. Until the integration has that guarantee, I prefer to make the uncertain state explicit.

The product demo shows the short scene this workflow supports. The same distinction between rejection, completion, and uncertainty is worth making anywhere a retry can start another paid job.

articles.title: Ubuntu Core Desktop Is Coming in 27.04 - And It Kills sudo apt (But Maybe That Is the Point?)
articles.description: I can't believe I'm saying this, but Ubuntu might be about to change for good.  Not a new wallpaper...
articles.body_html:
I can't believe I'm saying this, but Ubuntu might be about to change for good.

Not a new wallpaper kind of change. More like, you will not be able to install things the way you do now.

Canonical has restarted work on Ubuntu Core Desktop. It is a locked down, all-snap version of Ubuntu. And they want it to become the default Ubuntu. They already call the Ubuntu we use today "Classic Ubuntu." That name kind of gives it away, no? :)

Are we supposed to panic? I don't think so. But I do think we should look at it honestly before it lands in 27.04, which is about 6 months away.

So I went through the details. I am Taqui, I build web apps with Next.js and TypeScript, mostly full-stack stuff. One of my side projects is Wryte, a small AI blog writer I made for myself. So I read announcements like this with a normal user hat on, not an admin hat. Here is what I found.

Quick background

Ubuntu Core is not new. Canonical made it in 2015 for IoT, robots and industrial devices. Stuff you install once and never touch again. It worked well there.

Desktop was different. In 2023 they showed a first preview of Core Desktop. It was supposed to come in 2024, then it went quiet for 2 years.

Why? Their engineering chief John Seager said the preview was not good enough. They put almost the whole desktop in one giant base snap. That makes updates huge and swapping parts very hard.

That is just bad engineering, I guess they were in a hurry to show something.

Now a new team is splitting it into small pieces. Daily builds in the next few weeks.

Canonical actually posted the official announcement on Discourse here: Accelerating Ubuntu Core Desktop. It calls Core Desktop the most fundamental shift in Ubuntu desktop architecture so far. That post is where they explain the new split snap design.

How does it work

On normal Ubuntu, sudo apt update writes directly into your system folders. The OS changes itself.

On Core Desktop, the system is immutable. Read-only. That means the core cannot be broken by a bad package.

Think Lego, not like a recipe. There are 6 main blocks:

  1. gadget snap - bootloader, partitions, TPM encryption
  2. kernel snap - kernel and drivers
  3. boot base - minimal root filesystem
  4. snapd - updates and rollback
  5. system snaps - wifi, bluetooth, audio, power
  6. desktop and app snaps - GNOME / KDE and every app you install

Each snap is a compressed read-only file. Your home folder is separate and writable. If an update breaks, it rolls back on reboot.

Source: Inside Ubuntu Core docs

What I like about this is it is simple to explain. Want to update network without touching kernel? You can. That part makes sense to me.

How is this different from Fedora Silverblue

Silverblue and NixOS already do immutable stuff. But they are not beginner friendly. You have to learn RPM-OSTree, image layering, wikis, etc. Just to install something.

Core Desktop is trying to do the same thing, but with snaps, which Ubuntu users already know. So install feels familiar. That is the whole point, I think. Less learning curve.

So you cannot apt install?

Yes. That is the big one.

No sudo apt install on the host. No .deb packages on the base. No flatpak on the host either.

If it is not in the Snap Store, you are stuck. Even Canonical says this is the biggest problem right now.

So they are pushing three use cases for 27.04:

1. Browser focused PCs
Firefox and Chromium already work as snaps. Most of us live in the browser anyway, so for a lot of people this might already be enough.

2. Developer PCs
If the host is read-only, how do you code? Canonical says use containers. With LXD, Docker or their Workshop tool you can run a container in one command and inside you can apt install anything. Your app still shows on the desktop.

This part feels familiar to me, since I ship Next.js apps from a containerised setup myself sometimes. I get why they do it. It just does not feel as normal as installing directly. Not yet, at least.

3. Gaming PCs
They spent over a year on the Steam snap, with Proton and Mesa drivers inside. For Nvidia, there is a new gpu-2604 interface to deliver drivers via snaps.

Also, because kernel is a snap, you could switch to a gaming kernel in one command. That would be cool if it works.

And flavors? GNOME is not the only one. KDE, Budgie, MATE can all be swapped because the desktop is separate from the base. Canonical is already working with KDE on KDE Neon Core. Each snap has stable, candidate, beta, edge channels, so you could keep the base stable and test desktop on edge. That part I actually like :)

What happens to Classic Ubuntu

They say Classic Ubuntu is not going away yet. There is still a Debian team maintaining debs.

But John Seager also said his long term plan is to make Core the default for desktop, server and edge. For companies and governments that makes a lot of sense. They can deploy thousands of identical locked machines with up to 15 years support.

If that is where the money is, and best engineers move there, I think Classic will slowly fade. That is how Ubuntu has always moved - enterprise first, desktop follows.

My worry

For enterprise this is great. For people who like to tinker, it puts a wall between you and the machine.

One tester tried Core Desktop on a Steam Deck. Battery was bad, he wanted TLP and to edit a systemd file. On normal Ubuntu that is 10 seconds. On Core he was locked out.

Another tester, William, said the installer forced Ubuntu One login and TPM encryption. No choice. Once you are in, you cannot unsnap the OS or install debs on host. He said it felt more closed than Windows.

I get it. When everything is read-only, that Linux tinkering spirit goes away a bit. That is the part that worries me.

I am someone who sets up my PC once, installs my main apps, and never changes anything. For me, tiny updates that never break sound perfect. In theory it sounds great.

But I also started with Ubuntu because I could open a terminal and fix things myself. That freedom mattered.

Final thoughts

Core Desktop is not replacing Classic tomorrow. But the direction is clear. Canonical wants immutable, snap-first, enterprise-shaped. That is their future.

I do not know if it is good or bad yet. We will know when we actually try it.

So what do you think? Are you staying for this, or are you already packing for Debian or Mint? :)

If you want to read more, the Inside Ubuntu Core docs are actually readable, even for desktop users. And the official Accelerating Ubuntu Core Desktop thread on Ubuntu Discourse is the best place to follow daily builds. Worth a look :)
